title: Abstract Tate residue and its basic invariances
statement:
Let $k$ be a field, $C$ a commutative $k$-algebra, and $V$ a $C$-module. For $f\in C$ write $m_f(v)=fv$. Call a $k$-subspace $A\subseteq V$ admissible if $(m_f A+A)/A$ is finite-dimensional over $k$ for every $f\in C$. An endomorphism $T$ of a $k$-vector space is finite-potent if $T^N(V)$ is finite-dimensional for some $N\geq1$; its Tate trace $\operatorname{Tr}_{\mathrm{fp}}(T)$ is the ordinary trace on a finite-dimensional $T$-stable subspace containing $T^N(V)$, independent of these choices. For every admissible $A$ there is a unique $k$-linear map $\operatorname{res}_{V,A}:\Omega^1_{C/k}\to k$ [def-weil-pbc-kahler-differentials] such that for every $k$-linear projection $\pi:V\to A$ and every $f,g\in C$, the endomorphism $[\pi m_f,m_g]=\pi m_fm_g-m_g\pi m_f$ is finite-potent and
$$\operatorname{res}_{V,A}(f\,dg)=\operatorname{Tr}_{\mathrm{fp}}([\pi m_f,m_g]).$$
This residue is independent of $\pi$. It is unchanged under $C$-linear isomorphisms of pairs $(V,A)$. If $W\subseteq V$ is a $C$-submodule containing $A$, then $\operatorname{res}_{W,A}=\operatorname{res}_{V,A}$. If either $A$ or $V/A$ is finite-dimensional over $k$, then $\operatorname{res}_{V,A}=0$. If $m_f A\subseteq A$ and $m_g A\subseteq A$, then $\operatorname{res}_{V,A}(f\,dg)=0$; in particular $\operatorname{res}_{V,A}=0$ when $A$ is a $C$-submodule.

source.place: §1, properties T1–T5, pp. 149–151; §2, Theorem 1 and its finite commutator formula (*), p. 152, and properties R1–R2, pp. 152–153.

proof.text: Use [lem-pc-finite-potent-trace-calculus] for the well-defined finite-potent trace in the statement, including restriction/quotient additivity, cyclicity and its restricted additivity criterion. By [lem-trf-vector-subspace-complement] choose $V=A\oplus A'$ and let $\pi(a+a')=a$. This is a $k$-linear projection onto $A$, fixing $A$ pointwise; thus projections exist even when $A$ and $V$ have arbitrary dimension. Throughout, products of operators mean composition, with the right factor applied first.

source.place: §1, T1–T5, pp. 149–150; projection in Proposition 1, p. 151.

proof.text:
Use the operator algebra of [lem-pc-tate-endomorphism-ideals] for the subspace $A\subseteq V$. With $X\prec Y$ meaning that $(X+Y)/Y$ is finite-dimensional, equivalently $X\subseteq Y+U$ for a finite-dimensional $U$ (choose representatives of a finite basis), put
$$E=\{T:TA\prec A\},\quad E_1=\{T:TV\prec A\},\quad E_2=\{T:\dim_k TA<\infty\},\quad E_0=E_1\cap E_2.$$
These are exactly the subspaces of that node, which states that $E$ is a unital $k$-subalgebra of $\operatorname{End}_k(V)$ and that $E_1,E_2$ are two-sided ideals in $E$; in particular $E_1,E_2\subseteq E$, and a product with one factor in $E$ and one in $E_i$ lies in $E_i$, in either order. (Concretely, if $TA\subseteq A+U_T$, $SA\subseteq A+U_S$, then $TSA\subseteq A+U_T+TU_S$; if moreover $SV\subseteq A+U_S$ then $TSV\subseteq A+U_T+TU_S$ and $STV\subseteq SV$; if $SA$ is finite-dimensional then so are $TSA$ and $STA\subseteq SA+SU_T$.) Admissibility of $A$ says precisely that every $m_f$, $f\in C$, lies in $E$.

source.place: §1, definition of the E spaces and Proposition 1, p. 151; elementary verification of the ideal properties.

proof.text: By [lem-pc-tate-endomorphism-ideals], every element of $E_0$ is finite-potent and the finite-potent trace of [lem-pc-finite-potent-trace-calculus] is a $k$-linear function on $E_0$. (Directly: for $T,S\in E_0$ with $SV\subseteq A+U$, $TSV\subseteq TA+TU$ is finite-dimensional, so every pairwise product of members of $E_0$ has finite rank, and the restricted additivity and scalar formula of the trace node apply.) The same node gives the two trace-zero rules used below: if $T\in E_0$ and $S\in E$, or if $T\in E_1$ and $S\in E_2$, then $[T,S]\in E_0$ and $\operatorname{Tr}_{\mathrm{fp}}[T,S]=0$ (both $TS,ST$ lie in $E_0$, and cyclicity plus linearity on $E_0$ give zero). No additivity for arbitrary sums of finite-potent operators is being used.

source.place: §1, Propositions 1–2, p. 151, deduced explicitly from T4 in the pairwise finite-rank case and T5.

proof.text:
Call $F$ a lift of $f\in C$ if $F\in E_1$ and $F-m_f\in E_2$. For any projection $\pi$ onto $A$, $F=\pi m_f$ is a lift: its image is in $A$, and $(\pi-1)m_f(A)$ is finite-dimensional because $m_f(A)\subseteq A+U$ and $\pi-1$ kills $A$. Every lift belongs to $E$ since $E_1\subseteq E$. Lifts add and scale, and if $F,G$ lift $f,g$ then $FG$ lifts $fg$, since
$$FG-m_{fg}=(F-m_f)G+m_f(G-m_g)\in E_2.$$
Further, $[F,G]\in E_1$ by the ideal property of [lem-pc-tate-endomorphism-ideals], and $[F,G]\in E_2$ because reduction modulo $E_2$ gives $[m_f,m_g]=0$. Hence this commutator belongs to $E_0$ and is finite-potent by the preceding step.

source.place: §2, proof of Theorem 1, p. 151; explicit lift and ideal calculations.

proof.text: Define $q(f,g)=\operatorname{Tr}_{\mathrm{fp}}[F,G]$ using any two lifts in $E_1$. If $F'$ is another lift of $f$, then $F'-F\in E_0$. The difference of the two commutators is $[F'-F,G]$, whose trace is zero by the first trace-zero rule of [lem-pc-tate-endomorphism-ideals] (step 3). Linearity on $E_0$ therefore proves independence of $F$; interchanging the roles proves independence of $G$. Choosing lifts $\pi m_f,\pi m_g$ with one fixed projection, their separate linearity and trace linearity on $E_0$ prove that $q$ is $k$-bilinear. Also $q(f,f)=0$ by taking identical lifts. These are applications of the trace formulas in [lem-pc-finite-potent-trace-calculus] only in the cases checked in step 3.

source.place: §2, proof of Theorem 1, pp. 151–152; independence and bilinearity.

proof.text:
The formula with just one lifted operator is equally valid. For a lift $F$ of $f$ and $g\in C$, $[F,m_g]\in E_1\cap E_2$: use that $E_1$ is an ideal and that modulo $E_2$ the two multiplications commute. If $G$ lifts $g$, then $m_g-G\in E_2$ and
$$[F,m_g]-[F,G]=[F,m_g-G].$$
The second trace-zero rule of [lem-pc-tate-endomorphism-ideals] (step 3), followed by linearity on $E_0$, gives $q(f,g)=\operatorname{Tr}_{\mathrm{fp}}[F,m_g]$. In particular $q(f,c)=0$ for $c\in k$, because $m_c=c\operatorname{id}_V$ commutes with every $k$-linear $F$. Taking $F=\pi m_f$ proves both the finite-potence assertion and the exact projection formula required by the item, once the residue is constructed.

source.place: §2, Theorem 1 and the Remark preceding formula (*), p. 152.

proof.text:
Let $F,G,H$ lift $f,g,h$ in $E_1$. Products of lifts are lifts, and the operator identity
$$[F,GH]=[FG,H]+[HF,G]$$
is obtained by expanding and cancelling the terms $HFG$. All three commutators are in $E_0$ (step 4, using [lem-pc-tate-endomorphism-ideals]). The trace linearity of [lem-pc-finite-potent-trace-calculus] in step 3 consequently gives
$$q(f,gh)=q(fg,h)+q(fh,g).$$
Use the explicit free-$C$-module presentation of $\Omega^1_{C/k}$ in [def-weil-pbc-kahler-differentials]. On its free module define the $k$-linear functional $\sum_i f_i[g_i]\mapsto\sum_i q(f_i,g_i)$. Bilinearity makes it well-defined on coefficients. It kills every $C$-multiple of an additive relation by additivity in the second variable, every multiple of $[gh]-g[h]-h[g]$ by the displayed identity, and every multiple of $[c]$, $c\in k$, by step 6. It therefore descends to a $k$-linear functional $r:\Omega^1_{C/k}\to k$ with $r(f\,dg)=q(f,g)$. This uses precisely the presentation stated by the cited node, without assuming that $k$ is a $C$-module.

source.place: §2, proof of Theorem 1, pp. 151–152; descent through the differential relations, using the equivalent free-module presentation.

proof.text: The elements $f\,dg$ span $\Omega^1_{C/k}$ over $k$: every differential is a finite $C$-linear sum of $dg$ by the presentation in [def-weil-pbc-kahler-differentials], and each coefficient is absorbed into $f$. Thus the displayed values determine $r$ uniquely. Step 6 shows these values satisfy the required formula for every projection $\pi$, and step 5 shows they are independent of the choices. Write this unique functional as $\operatorname{res}_{V,A}$.

For the ambient-space invariance, write out Tate's finite computation. Fix $f,g$ and a projection $\pi$, and put
$$B=A+m_gA,\qquad D=B\cap m_f^{-1}(A)\cap m_{fg}^{-1}(A),\qquad S=[\pi m_f,m_g].$$
The quotient $B/A$ is finite-dimensional. The linear map $B\to(V/A)\oplus(V/A)$ sending $v$ to $(fv\bmod A,fgv\bmod A)$ has kernel $D$ and finite-dimensional image: its components are contained in $(fA+fgA+A)/A$ and $(fgA+fg^2A+A)/A$, respectively, both finite-dimensional by admissibility. Choosing representatives of a basis of that image shows $B/D$ is finite-dimensional. Moreover $S(V)\subseteq B$, and $S(D)=0$, since for $v\in D$ both $fv,fgv$ lie in $A$ and hence $S(v)=fgv-gfv=0$. Apply restriction/quotient additivity in [lem-pc-finite-potent-trace-calculus] first to $B\subseteq V$, then to $D\subseteq B$. The induced endomorphism on $V/B$ and the restriction to $D$ are zero, so
$$\operatorname{res}_{V,A}(f\,dg)=\operatorname{Tr}_k(\overline S\mid B/D).$$
This is formula (*) with its finite-dimensionality and all stable-subspace hypotheses verified.

source.place: §2, Remark and finite formula (*), p. 152; restriction/quotient form of T2.

proof.text: If $W\subseteq V$ is a $C$-submodule containing $A$, it is admissible as an ambient module because $(m_fA+A)/A$ is the same vector space. Restrict any projection $\pi:V\to A$ to $W$. The spaces $B,D$ of step 9 lie in $W$ and are unchanged, and the operator induced on $B/D$ is unchanged. Hence step 9 gives equal residues on each $f\,dg$; their spanning property from [def-weil-pbc-kahler-differentials] gives $\operatorname{res}_{W,A}=\operatorname{res}_{V,A}$.

source.place: §2, R1, p. 152; the finite computation above realizes the ambient restriction assertion.

proof.text: Let $u:V\to V'$ be a $C$-linear isomorphism with $u(A)=A'$. Admissibility transfers because $u(m_fA+A)=m_fA'+A'$. The conjugate $\pi'=u\pi u^{-1}$ projects onto $A'$, and its commutator is $S'=uSu^{-1}$. To compare traces, use cyclicity from [lem-pc-finite-potent-trace-calculus] with $a=u$ and $b=Su^{-1}$, so $ba=S$ and $ab=S'$. The traces, and therefore the residues of $f\,dg$, coincide. Spanning, as in step 8, proves invariance of the complete functionals.

source.place: §1, T5, p. 150; §2, definition of residue and R1, pp. 151–152.

proof.text: If $A$ is finite-dimensional, the zero operator is a lift of every $f$: its image is zero and $(0-m_f)(A)$ is finite-dimensional. Using two zero lifts gives $q(f,g)=0$. If $V/A$ is finite-dimensional, choose finitely many representatives for a quotient basis, giving $V=A+U$ for finite-dimensional $U$. Admissibility gives $m_fA\subseteq A+U_f$, so $m_fV\subseteq A+U_f+m_fU$. Thus $m_f\in E_1$, and $m_f$ itself is a lift of $f$. The two original multiplications commute, so again $q(f,g)=0$. In each case $\operatorname{res}=0$ by step 8. In the second case one can also use $V\prec A$ to see $m_fV\prec A$ immediately.

source.place: §2, consequence of R1 and the lift characterization; vanishing for finite-dimensional or finite-codimensional A.

proof.text:
Finally suppose $fA\subseteq A$ and $gA\subseteq A$. Take lifts $F=m_f\pi$ and $G=m_g\pi$: their images lie in $A$, and $F-m_f$ and $G-m_g$ vanish on $A$, so they lie in $E_2$. For every $v$, both $g\pi v$ and $f\pi v$ lie in $A$, and therefore
$$FGv=fg\pi v=gf\pi v=GFv.$$
Thus $q(f,g)=0$. If $A$ is a $C$-submodule, this applies to every $f,g$; step 8 gives $\operatorname{res}_{V,A}=0$. This works in every characteristic and uses no division by $2$.

source.place: §2, R2, pp. 152–153; direct commuting-lift verification of the required special case.

proof_origin.place: §1 T1–T5 and Propositions 1–2; §2 Theorem 1, formula (*), and R1–R2, pp. 149–153.
